orig_sentences: All those lives maintained in the rarefied air of the absurd could not persevere without some profound and constant thought to infuse its strength into them.
Right here, it can be only a strange feeling of fidelity.
Conscious men have been seen to fulfill their task amid the most stupid of wars without considering themselves in contradiction.
This is because it was essential to elude nothing.
There is thus a metaphysical honor in enduring the world’s absurdity.
Conquest or play-acting, multiple loves, absurd revolt are tributes that man pays to his dignity in a campaign in which he is defeated in advance.
mod_sentences: All lives sustained within the rarefied atmosphere of the absurd would quickly collapse without some deep, steadfast conviction to lend them endurance.
Here, that conviction can only be a peculiar sense of fidelity.
Lucid men have carried out their duties in the midst of the most senseless wars without sensing any contradiction in their conduct.
This is because their primary obligation was to evade nothing.
There is an undeniable metaphysical honor in enduring the absurdity of the world.
Conquest, theatrical performance, numerous loves, and absurd defiance are the tributes human beings pay to their own dignity in a struggle where defeat is guaranteed from the outset.
pairs.move: Camus defines 'metaphysical honor': conscious persistence in an unwinnable struggle. The absurd archetypes (the conqueror, the actor, Don Juan) do not persist expecting salvation; their dignity lies precisely in maintaining lucid defiance in a campaign already lost.

orig_sentences: It is merely a matter of being faithful to the rule of the battle.
That thought may suffice to sustain a mind; it has supported and still supports whole civilizations.
War cannot be negated.
One must live it or die of it.
So it is with the absurd: it is a question of breathing with it, of recognizing its lessons and recovering their flesh.
In this regard the absurd joy par excellence is creation.
“Art and nothing but art,” said Nietzsche; “we have art in order not to die of the truth.”
mod_sentences: It is simply a matter of honoring the rules of engagement.
That single principle can sustain a mind; indeed, it has anchored entire civilizations.
War cannot be wished away.
One must either endure it or perish from it.
So it is with the absurd: one must learn to breathe within it, heed its instruction, and give tangible flesh to its insights.
In this respect, the supreme absurd joy is artistic creation.
As Nietzsche famously declared: 'Art and nothing but art; we have art so that we do not perish from the truth.'
pairs.move: Artistic creation as the supreme absurd triumph. Just as one cannot pretend war does not exist, one cannot wish away cosmic meaninglessness. Creation is the lucid refusal to flee reality while transforming cold truth into vital form.

orig_sentences: In the experience that I am attempting to describe and to stress on several modes, it is certain that a new torment arises wherever another dies.
The childish chasing after forgetfulness, the appeal of satisfaction are now devoid of echo.
But the constant tension that keeps man face to face with the world, the ordered delirium that urges him to be receptive to everything leave him another fever.
In this universe the work of art is then the sole chance of keeping his consciousness and of fixing its adventures.
Creating is living doubly.
The groping, anxious quest of a Proust, his meticulous collecting of flowers, of wallpapers, and of anxieties, signifies nothing else.
At the same time, it has no more significance than the continual and imperceptible creation in which the actor, the conqueror, and all absurd men indulge every day of their lives.
All try their hands at miming, at repeating, and at re-creating the reality that is theirs.
We always end up by having the appearance of our truths.
All existence for a man turned away from the eternal is but a vast mime under the mask of the absurd.
Creation is the great mime.
mod_sentences: In the lived experience I am exploring across its various forms, whenever one torment subsides, another inevitably takes its place.
The naive scramble for distraction and the craving for permanent comfort no longer resonate.
Yet the unyielding tension confronting man with the universe—this disciplined delirium compelling him to welcome every sensation—ignites a new fever within him.
Within such an existence, the work of art represents the sole vehicle for sustaining consciousness and recording its trials.
To create is to live twice over.
The tentative, agonizing quest of Marcel Proust—his obsessive cataloging of hawthorn blossoms, vintage wallpapers, and inner anxieties—expresses nothing less.
Simultaneously, it possesses no more ultimate cosmic importance than the ongoing, silent self-creation performed daily by the actor, the conqueror, and every lucid individual.
All of them strive to mimic, rehearse, and recreate the immediate reality allotted to them.
In the end, we inevitably take on the physical shape of the truths we inhabit.
For anyone who has turned away from the illusion of eternity, life is merely a vast performance under the mask of the absurd.
Artistic creation is the consummate mime.
pairs.move: Creation as 'living doubly' without claiming cosmic superiority. Proust's grand novel has no more eternal merit than an actor's fleeting gesture or a lover's passion. Art is not an eternal monument, but a lucid mime of mortal experience.

orig_sentences: Such men know to begin with, and then their whole effort is to examine, to enlarge, and to enrich the ephemeral island on which they have just landed.
But first they must know.
For the absurd discovery coincides with a pause in which future passions are prepared and justified.
Even men without a gospel have their Mount of Olives.
And one must not fall asleep on theirs either.
For the absurd man it is not a matter of explaining and solving, but of experiencing and describing.
Everything begins with lucid indifference.
mod_sentences: Such men begin with awareness, and their subsequent labor is to explore, expand, and cultivate the transient island upon which they have been cast.
Yet consciousness must come first.
The revelation of the absurd marks a reflective pause during which future passions are forged and validated.
Even those who recognize no gospel endure their own Garden of Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives.
And they, too, are forbidden to slumber during the watch.
For the absurd mind, the task is never to explain or resolve existence, but to experience and describe it.
Everything originates in lucid indifference.
pairs.move: The shift from explanation to description. The absurd thinker does not solve the riddle of the universe; like Christ on the Mount of Olives, he stays awake during the vigil of mortal isolation. The goal is descriptive fidelity rather than metaphysical dogma.

orig_sentences: Describing—that is the last ambition of an absurd thought.
Science likewise, having reached the end of its paradoxes, ceases to propound and stops to contemplate and sketch the ever virgin landscape of phenomena.
The heart learns thus that the emotion delighting us when we see the world’s aspects comes to us not from its depth but from their diversity.
Explanation is useless, but the sensation remains and, with it, the constant attractions of a universe inexhaustible in quantity.
The place of the work of art can be understood at this point.
mod_sentences: Description remains the ultimate ambition of absurd thought.
Science itself, once driven to the outer boundary of its paradoxes, abandons metaphysical speculation to observe and map the pristine landscape of physical phenomena.
The soul discovers that the joy we derive from contemplating the world springs not from some hidden cosmic depth, but from sheer sensory diversity.
While explanations prove futile, sensory experience endures, accompanied by the endless allure of a universe inexhaustible in its sheer volume.
It is here that the true role of the work of art becomes evident.
pairs.move: Phenomenology over metaphysics. Camus aligns absurd philosophy with empirical science: both abandon claims of deciphering ultimate essences and instead document surface appearances and quantitative variety.

orig_sentences: It marks both the death of an experience and its multiplication.
It is a sort of monotonous and passionate repetition of the themes already orchestrated by the world: the body, inexhaustible image on the pediment of temples, forms or colors, number or grief.
It is therefore not indifferent, as a conclusion, to encounter once again the principal themes of this essay in the wonderful and childish world of the creator.
It would be wrong to see a symbol in it and to think that the work of art can be considered at last as a refuge for the absurd.
It is itself an absurd phenomenon, and we are concerned merely with its description.
It does not offer an escape for the intellectual ailment.
Rather, it is one of the symptoms of that ailment which reflects it throughout a man’s whole thought.
But for the first time it makes the mind get outside of itself and places it in opposition to others, not for it to get lost but to show it clearly the blind path that all have entered upon.
In the time of the absurd reasoning, creation follows indifference and discovery.
It marks the point from which absurd passions spring and where the reasoning stops.
Its place in this essay is justified in this way.
mod_sentences: The work of art signals both the culmination of an experience and its vibrant multiplication.

It constitutes a passionate, rhythmic repetition of themes already sounded by the world: the human body, endlessly sculpted upon temple pediments, the interplay of forms and hues, mathematical order and human grief.
It is entirely fitting, therefore, that the core themes of this inquiry reappear within the marvelous, uncomplicated realm of artistic creation.
Yet it would be an error to treat art as a transcendent symbol or to mistake the artistic work for an escape hatch from absurdity.
Art is itself an absurd phenomenon, and our responsibility is simply to describe it.
It provides no cure for the intellectual malady.
Instead, it is a primary symptom of that condition, projecting the crisis across the entire canvas of human thought.
Yet for the first time, creation compels the mind to venture beyond its private borders and confront the world, not to lose itself, but to illuminate the dead-end path upon which all mortals tread.
Within the trajectory of absurd reasoning, creation succeeds discovery and detached contemplation.
It marks the exact threshold where absurd passions erupt and abstract deduction reaches its limit.
This alone justifies its presence in this essay.
pairs.move: Art is a symptom of the absurd, not a cure. Camus warns against treating art as secular salvation. The artwork does not redeem our mortality; it merely externalizes and dramatizes our shared confrontation with the void.

orig_sentences: It will suffice to bring to light a few themes common to the creator and the thinker in order to find in the work of art all the contradictions of thought involved in the absurd.
Indeed, it is not so much identical conclusions that prove minds to be related as the contradictions that are common to them.
So it is with thought and creation.
I hardly need to say that the same anguish urges man to these two attitudes.
This is where they coincide in the beginning.
But among all the thoughts that start from the absurd, I have seen that very few remain within it.
And through their deviations or infidelities I have best been able to measure what belonged to the absurd.
Similarly I must wonder: is an absurd work of art possible?
mod_sentences: It will be enough to illuminate several themes shared by the creator and the philosopher to uncover within art every contradiction inherent in absurd thought.
Indeed, what binds kindred minds together is not a shared set of doctrines, but the shared paradoxes they wrestle with.
Such is the kinship between contemplation and artistic creation.
Both stances, it goes without saying, are propelled by the identical existential anguish.
At their origin, they are one.
Yet among all the philosophies that commence with the absurd, very few maintain their fidelity to it.
It was through their evasions and intellectual betrayals that I was able to chart the exact boundaries of the absurd.
Now I must pose an identical question: Is an authentically absurd work of art possible?
pairs.move: The shared origin of philosophy and art, and the core test: Can an artwork remain absurd without betraying its premises through false transcendence or smuggled hope?

orig_sentences: It would be impossible to insist too much on the arbitrary nature of the former opposition between art and philosophy.
If you insist on taking it in too limited a sense, it is certainly false.
If you mean merely that these two disciplines each have their peculiar climate, that is probably true but remains vague.
The only acceptable argument used to lie in the contradiction brought up between the philosopher enclosed within his system and the artist placed before his work.
But this was pertinent for a certain form of art and of philosophy which we consider secondary here.
The idea of an art detached from its creator is not only outmoded; it is false.
In opposition to the artist, it is pointed out that no philosopher ever created several systems.
But that is true in so far, indeed, as no artist ever expressed more than one thing under different aspects.
The instantaneous perfection of art, the necessity for its renewal—this is true only through a preconceived notion.
For the work of art likewise is a construction and everyone knows how monotonous the great creators can be.
For the same reason as the thinker, the artist commits himself and becomes himself in his work.
That osmosis raises the most important of æsthetic problems.
Moreover, to anyone who is convinced of the mind’s singleness of purpose, nothing is more futile than these distinctions based on methods and objects.
There are no frontiers between the disciplines that man sets himself for understanding and loving.
They interlock, and the same anxiety merges them.
mod_sentences: One cannot emphasize too strongly how artificial the traditional divide between art and philosophy truly is.
Understood in a narrow, dogmatic sense, the distinction is entirely unfounded.
If one simply means that each discipline possesses its own distinctive atmosphere, that may be conceded, though it remains a vague observation.
The only defensible historical argument contrasted the philosopher locked within a theoretical system against the artist standing directly before their canvas.
Yet that contrast applied only to certain historical forms of art and philosophy that are irrelevant to our inquiry.
The notion of art existing in sterile detachment from its maker is not merely obsolete; it is fundamentally false.
Critics often claim, against the artist, that no philosopher ever constructed more than one system.
Yet that holds true only to the extent that no genuine artist ever articulates more than a single core reality across diverse forms.
The belief that art achieves spontaneous perfection while constantly reinventing itself is an unexamined myth.
A work of art is a painstaking construction, and every perceptive reader knows how relentlessly consistent—even monotonous—the greatest creators can be.
Like the philosopher, the artist commits their entire existence to their work and discovers their identity through it.
This profound synthesis raises the fundamental question of aesthetics.
Furthermore, to anyone aware of the mind's essential unity, few exercises are more pointless than scholastic debates over academic boundaries and methodologies.
No rigid borders divide the disciplines human beings devise to comprehend and cherish existence.
They intertwine, fused together by the identical existential anxiety.
pairs.move: Dismantling the false dichotomy between art and philosophy. Both thinkers and artists express a single central vision through iterative variation. System-building in philosophy and world-building in fiction are driven by the same human impulse to master reality.

orig_sentences: It is necessary to state this to begin with.
For an absurd work of art to be possible, thought in its most lucid form must be involved in it.
But at the same time thought must not be apparent except as the regulating intelligence.
This paradox can be explained according to the absurd.
The work of art is born of the intelligence’s refusal to reason the concrete.
It marks the triumph of the carnal.
It is lucid thought that provokes it, but in that very act that thought repudiates itself.
It will not yield to the temptation of adding to what is described a deeper meaning that it knows to be illegitimate.
The work of art embodies a drama of the intelligence, but it proves this only indirectly.
The absurd work requires an artist conscious of these limitations and an art in which the concrete signifies nothing more than itself.
It cannot be the end, the meaning, and the consolation of a life.
Creating or not creating changes nothing.
The absurd creator does not prize his work.
He could repudiate it.
He does sometimes repudiate it.
An Abyssinia suffices for this, as in the case of Rimbaud.
mod_sentences: This foundational premise must be stated clearly.
If an absurd work of art is to be realized, the intellect must be present in its most razor-sharp clarity.
Yet at the same time, that intellect must never show itself except as the guiding, restraining hand.
This apparent paradox is resolved through the logic of the absurd.
The artwork is born when reason deliberately refuses to rationalize the concrete world.
It represents the victory of physical, sensory reality.
Lucid intellect initiates the creative act, yet in that very gesture, reason abdicates its claim to explain.
It resists the seductive urge to impose an artificial, transcendent meaning upon what it depicts—a meaning it knows to be illegitimate.
The work of art reflects an intellectual drama, but it testifies to this conflict only indirectly.
An absurd work demands an artist acutely aware of these boundaries, producing an art where physical reality signifies nothing beyond itself.
It can never serve as the ultimate purpose, the meaning, or the consoling prize of an existence.
Whether one creates or abandons creation alters nothing fundamental.
The absurd artist refuses to idolize their own output.
They remain capable of renouncing it entirely.
Indeed, they sometimes do walk away.
A flight to Abyssinia is sufficient, as Rimbaud proved.
pairs.move: The aesthetic paradox of the absurd: Art is born when lucid intellect intentionally surrenders its impulse to explain, allowing physical reality to speak without symbolic baggage. The creator maintains absolute detachment, ready to abandon art entirely (like Rimbaud fleeing to Africa).

orig_sentences: At the same time a rule of æsthetics can be seen in this.
The true work of art is always on the human scale.
It is essentially the one that says “less.”
There is a certain relationship between the global experience of the artist and the work that reflects that experience, between Wilhelm Meister and Goethe’s maturity.
That relationship is bad when the work aims to give the whole experience in the lace-paper of an explanatory literature.
That relationship is good when the work is but a piece cut out of experience, a facet of the diamond in which the inner luster is epitomized without being limited.
In the first case there is overloading and pretension to the eternal.
In the second, a fecund work because of a whole implied experience, the wealth of which is suspected.
The problem for the absurd artist is to acquire this savoir-vivre which transcends savoir-faire.
And in the end, the great artist under this climate is, above all, a great living being, it being understood that living in this case is just as much experiencing as reflecting.
The work then embodies an intellectual drama.
The absurd work illustrates thought’s renouncing of its prestige and its resignation to being no more than the intelligence that works up appearances and covers with images what has no reason.
If the world were clear, art would not exist.
mod_sentences: Simultaneously, a fundamental aesthetic principle emerges from this stance.
The genuine work of art remains strictly on a human scale.
Above all, it is the work that practices restraint—the art that says 'less.'
A delicate relationship links an artist’s total life experience to the creation reflecting it, such as the bond between Wilhelm Meister and Goethe’s mature years.
That relationship falters when an author attempts to package their entire philosophy inside the ornate wrapping of an explanatory novel.
The relationship succeeds when the artwork is merely a carved fragment of lived experience—a single facet of a diamond whose inner radiance is concentrated without being confined.
In the first instance, one finds intellectual clutter and an arrogant claim to eternal truth.
In the second, one discovers a fertile work rich with tacit experience, whose hidden depth is felt rather than preached.
The challenge for the absurd artist is to cultivate this wisdom of living that transcends mere technical craft.
Ultimately, a great creator in this landscape is first and foremost a fully alive human being—understanding that living demands both raw experience and lucid reflection.
The work then embodies a profound drama of the mind.

The absurd creation dramatizes thought surrendering its royal pretensions, accepting its modest role as the craftsman that shapes appearances and garments in vivid imagery that which has no cosmic reason.
If the world were transparent, art would not exist.
pairs.move: The art of saying 'less' and the aphorism 'If the world were clear, art would not exist.' Great art is restrained, concrete, and unpretentious; it exists solely because the universe is opaque and refuses to yield rational answers.

orig_sentences: I am not speaking here of the arts of form or color in which description alone prevails in its splendid modesty.
Expression begins where thought ends.
Those adolescents with empty eyesockets who people temples and museums—their philosophy has been expressed in gestures.
For an absurd man it is more educative than all libraries.
Under another aspect the same is true for music.
If any art is devoid of lessons, it is certainly music.
It is too closely related to mathematics not to have borrowed their gratuitousness.

That game the mind plays with itself according to set and measured laws takes place in the sonorous compass that belongs to us and beyond which the vibrations nevertheless meet in an inhuman universe.
There is no purer sensation.
These examples are too easy.
The absurd man recognizes as his own these harmonies and these forms.
mod_sentences: I am not referring here to painting or sculpture, where pure visual depiction reigns with magnificent modesty.
Genuine artistic expression begins precisely where didactic thought ends.
The ancient statues of hollow-eyed youths populating temples and museums express their philosophy through posture and gesture alone.
For an absurd observer, those mute figures offer deeper instruction than entire libraries of theory.
In a different register, the identical truth governs music.
If any art form is entirely free of moralizing lectures, it is surely music.
It is too intimately bound to mathematics not to have inherited its pure, non-utilitarian freedom.
That rhythmic game the mind plays with sound according to strict laws unfolds within a human acoustic boundary, beyond which sound waves dissolve into an indifferent universe.
No sensation is purer.
Yet these examples are almost too obvious.
The absurd individual readily recognizes their own spirit in these harmonies and sculptural forms.
pairs.move: Pure form vs. thesis: Visual art and music achieve absurd purity effortlessly because they convey no doctrinal lessons; their meaning resides entirely in surface rhythm and physical form.

orig_sentences: But I should like to speak here of a work in which the temptation to explain remains greatest, in which illusion offers itself automatically, in which conclusion is almost inevitable.
I mean fictional creation.
I propose to inquire whether or not the absurd can hold its own there.
mod_sentences: Instead, I want to examine an art form where the temptation to explain is overwhelming, where comforting illusions present themselves at every turn, and where moral conclusions seem almost unavoidable.
I speak of fiction.
My purpose is to determine whether the absurd can preserve its integrity within the novel.
pairs.move: The novel as the supreme acid test for absurd philosophy. Unlike music or sculpture, fiction constantly tempts the writer to moralize, explain, and fabricate artificial resolutions.

orig_sentences: To think is first of all to create a world (or to limit one’s own world, which comes to the same thing).

It is starting out from the basic disagreement that separates man from his experience in order to find a common ground according to one’s nostalgia, a universe hedged with reasons or lighted up with analogies but which, in any case, gives an opportunity to rescind the unbearable divorce.
The philosopher, even if he is Kant, is a creator.
He has his characters, his symbols, and his secret action.
He has his plot endings.
On the contrary, the lead taken by the novel over poetry and the essay merely represents, despite appearances, a greater intellectualization of the art.
Let there be no mistake about it; I am speaking of the greatest.
The fecundity and the importance of a literary form are often measured by the trash it contains.
The number of bad novels must not make us forget the value of the best.
These, indeed, carry with them their universe.
The novel has its logic, its reasonings, its intuition, and its postulates.
It also has its requirements of clarity.
mod_sentences: To think is, first and foremost, to construct a world—or to delineate the boundaries of one's own, which amounts to the same thing.

It means beginning with the fundamental rift dividing man from his experience, striving to establish common ground shaped by our longing—a cosmos fortified with rational explanations or illuminated by analogies, designed above all to annul this unbearable divorce.
Every philosopher, even an architect of systems like Immanuel Kant, is fundamentally a novelist of ideas.
He invents his dramatis personae, his conceptual symbols, and his hidden dramatic stakes.
He arranges his dramatic conclusions.
Conversely, the historical dominance of the novel over poetry and the essay reflects, contrary to superficial appearances, a profound intellectualization of storytelling.
Make no mistake: I am speaking exclusively of the greatest novelists.
The vitality and cultural weight of any literary genre are often judged by the mountains of mediocre pulp produced in its name.
Yet the deluge of bad fiction must never blind us to the supreme worth of the masterpiece.
Great novels carry an entire, self-contained universe within them.
The novel possesses its own rigorous logic, its dialectical arguments, its intuitive leaps, and its foundational axioms.
It also imposes its own demanding standards of clarity.
pairs.move: Philosophers are creators of fiction; great novelists are builders of philosophical worlds. Kant's categories are conceptual characters in a drama designed to repair the rift between mind and world.

orig_sentences: The classical opposition of which I was speaking above is even less justified in this particular case.
It held in the time when it was easy to separate philosophy from its authors.

Today when thought has ceased to lay claim to the universal, when its best history would be that of its repentances, we know that the system, when it is worth while, cannot be separated from its author.
The Ethics itself, in one of its aspects, is but a long and reasoned personal confession.
Abstract thought at last returns to its prop of flesh.
And, likewise, the fictional activities of the body and of the passions are regulated a little more according to the requirements of a vision of the world.
The writer has given up telling “stories” and creates his universe.
The great novelists are philosophical novelists—that is, the contrary of thesis-writers.
For instance, Balzac, Sade, Melville, Stendhal, Dostoevsky, Proust, Malraux, Kafka, to cite but a few.
mod_sentences: The historic opposition between philosopher and artist is even less defensible here.
It survived only as long as people could naively divorce an abstract philosophy from the living person who conceived it.

Today, when thought has abandoned its pretension to universal systems—and when the truest history of philosophy is simply the chronicle of its own retractions—we recognize that no significant system can ever be severed from its creator.
Even Spinoza’s Ethics, viewed from this angle, is essentially a long, reasoned personal confession.
Abstract thought finally returns to its anchor in human flesh.
Similarly, the fictional movements of characters’ bodies and passions are disciplined to serve a coherent vision of reality.
The serious writer no longer merely tells entertaining tales; they build a distinct universe.
The supreme novelists are philosophical novelists—the exact opposite of didactic thesis-writers.
Consider Balzac, Sade, Melville, Stendhal, Dostoevsky, Proust, Malraux, and Kafka, to name only a handful.
pairs.move: Philosophy as flesh-and-blood confession. Abstract systems are personal confessions of living men (even Spinoza). The great philosophical novelists (Dostoevsky, Melville, Kafka) do not write didactic propaganda; they embody metaphysical visions in carnal drama.

orig_sentences: But in fact the preference they have shown for writing in images rather than in reasoned arguments is revelatory of a certain thought that is common to them all, convinced of the uselessness of any principle of explanation and sure of the educative message of perceptible appearance.
They consider the work of art both as an end and a beginning.
It is the outcome of an often unexpressed philosophy, its illustration and its consummation.
But it is complete only through the implications of that philosophy.
It justifies at last that variant of an old theme that a little thought estranges from life whereas much thought reconciles to life.
Incapable of refining the real, thought pauses to mimic it.
The novel in question is the instrument of that simultaneously relative and inexhaustible knowledge, so like that of love.
Of love, fictional creation has the initial wonder and the fecund rumination.
mod_sentences: Their choice to write in concrete imagery rather than abstract syllogisms reveals a conviction shared by them all: that ultimate explanatory theories are useless, and that physical appearance carries a profound, instructive power.
They view the work of art simultaneously as a culmination and a genesis.
It is the fruit of an implicit philosophy—its living demonstration and its fulfillment.
Yet it attains completeness only through the unspoken weight of that worldview.
This art validates an ancient maxim: a little philosophy detaches us from life, whereas profound contemplation returns us directly to it.
Powerless to transcend the real, thought pauses simply to recreate it.
The novel becomes the instrument of a knowledge that is both relative and inexhaustible, remarkably akin to the knowledge discovered in love.
Like love, the creation of fiction begins with initial wonder and deepens through fertile, unending contemplation.
pairs.move: Thinking in images rather than syllogisms. 'A little thought estranges from life; much thought reconciles to life.' Great fiction abandons metaphysical abstractions to recreate the physical real, acting like love: inexhaustible, relative, and anchored in wonder.

orig_sentences: These at least are the charms I see in it at the outset.
But I saw them likewise in those princes of humiliated thought whose suicides I was later able to witness.
What interests me, indeed, is knowing and describing the force that leads them back toward the common path of illusion.
The same method will consequently help me here.
The fact of having already utilized it will allow me to shorten my argument and to sum it up without delay in a particular example.
I want to know whether, accepting a life without appeal, one can also agree to work and create without appeal and what is the way leading to these liberties.
I want to liberate my universe of its phantoms and to people it solely with flesh-and-blood truths whose presence I cannot deny.
I can perform absurd work, choose the creative attitude rather than another.
But an absurd attitude, if it is to remain so, must remain aware of its gratuitousness.
So it is with the work of art.
If the commandments of the absurd are not respected, if the work does not illustrate divorce and revolt, if it sacrifices to illusions and arouses hope, it ceases to be gratuitous.
I can no longer detach myself from it.
My life may find a meaning in it, but that is trifling.
It ceases to be that exercise in detachment and passion which crowns the splendor and futility of a man’s life.
mod_sentences: Such, at least, are the promises I perceive in fiction from the start.
Yet I once recognized identical promises in those brilliant existential thinkers whose philosophical suicides I was forced to witness.
What compels my attention is identifying and describing the insidious force that lures them back into the comforting traps of illusion.
The identical method of analysis will serve me here.
Having already established this critique, I can compress my argument and test it immediately against a concrete literary masterpiece.
My question is this: having accepted a mortal existence without cosmic appeal, can one also resolve to labor and create without appeal, and what path leads to such freedom?
I want to rid my world of supernatural specters and populate it exclusively with tangible, flesh-and-blood truths whose presence cannot be disputed.
I can engage in absurd labor and choose the creative path over any other.
Yet an absurd posture, if it is to maintain its integrity, must remain perpetually conscious of its own ultimate pointlessness.
The exact same law applies to the work of art.

If the core demands of the absurd are violated—if the novel fails to dramatize mortal estrangement and defiance, if it surrenders to illusion and rekindles metaphysical hope—it loses its radical gratuitousness.
I can no longer hold myself detached from it.
My life might seek shelter in its manufactured meaning, but that is a cheap consolation.
It ceases to be that supreme exercise in passion and detachment that crowns both the splendor and the futility of human existence.
pairs.move: Creating 'without appeal.' The central aesthetic thesis: Can an artist produce a masterpiece while consciously refusing to smuggle in hope or eternal meaning? If art becomes an idol or an ideological crutch, it forfeits its absurd purity.

orig_sentences: In the creation in which the temptation to explain is the strongest, can one overcome that temptation?
In the fictional world in which awareness of the real world is keenest, can I remain faithful to the absurd without sacrificing to the desire to judge?
So many questions to be taken into consideration in a last effort.
It must be already clear what they signify.
They are the last scruples of an awareness that fears to forsake its initial and difficult lesson in favor of a final illusion.
What holds for creation, looked upon as one of the possible attitudes for the man conscious of the absurd, holds for all the styles of life open to him.
mod_sentences: In the creative act, where the temptation to explain is most seductive, can an artist master and suppress that urge?
Within the imaginary landscape of fiction, where our grasp of the concrete world is at its sharpest, can I stay loyal to the absurd without yielding to the impulse to pass moral judgment?
These are the demanding questions that must be confronted in this final effort.
Their significance is already evident.
They represent the final misgivings of a consciousness terrified of trading its hard-won clarity for one last comforting illusion.
And whatever applies to artistic creation—considered here as one possible posture for the absurd individual—applies equally to every other path of life open to human freedom.
